# Driving this engine

A flow is not a list of instructions you follow — it is a state machine. Each step asks
for specific evidence, and the engine decides from the store whether it may close.

**This is the portable reference copy**: the path below is a placeholder, and a
machine-local copy with a working path is what an agent should actually read.

Produce one with `harness brief --write`.

This installation is a source checkout, so the command is not on your PATH:

```sh
alias harness='<path-to-engine>/bin/harness'
```

Everything below uses `harness`.

## Exit codes are the contract

| code | means | what you do |
|---|---|---|
| **0** | passed | carry on |
| **1** | bad usage, or an environment that cannot answer | fix the command, or the environment it names |
| **2** | the flow could not be loaded — invalid, or its extension code is not approved on this machine | read stderr. If it names an unapproved extension file, that is a LOCAL decision for whoever owns this machine (`harness trust`), not something to report or work around. Otherwise report it upstream; either way do NOT edit the spec to get past it |
| **3** | a rule is not satisfied | read stderr — it names what is missing and the command that supplies it |
| **4** | a protected action has no recorded authorisation | get a real human affirmation. Do NOT reword the action to slip past |
| **5** | the engine failed in a way it does not account for | report it with the traceback; this is a defect in the engine, not your input |

The refusal codes are products, not errors: their stderr names the exact remedy. Follow
it rather than inventing one.

## The loop

```sh
harness init                                                 # once; safe to repeat
harness abilities                                            # what is installed here
harness open <ability> --scope <key> --run <id>              # start a run
harness next --run <id>                                      # the next step, and what it requires
harness evidence --run <id> --step <s> --kind <k> --value <v> # record what the step asks for
harness close-step --run <id> --step <s>                     # refused if the criterion is unmet
harness close-run --run <id> --result <r>                    # refused while anything is owed
```

Diagnosis, all read-only:

```sh
harness status         # show a run, or all open runs
harness obligations    # list this run's obligations
harness assert-goal    # check whether a phase meets its acceptance criterion
harness show           # print a step's guide section, or one of its topics
harness validate       # validate flow spec(s); exit 2 if invalid
harness audit          # list unwitnessed gates and violations
harness leases         # show delegated scopes
harness history        # list runs that have ended
```

## What `next` gives you

Read the requirement lines and the directive. The guide and topic lines are POINTERS
— fetch them only when you need them (`harness show --run <id> --step C00`).

## Some steps hand something back

A step may declare an OUTPUT: a path you recorded as evidence, which the engine reads
and returns the declared part of when the step closes. `close-step --json` carries it;
the text form prints one line about it.

It is a channel, not a criterion. Failing to read it NEVER changes whether the step
closed — so do not treat a delivered excerpt as proof of anything. The status is one of
delivered / no_source_recorded / source_missing / selector_no_match / unreadable, and
'could not read it' is deliberately not the same answer as 'it was empty'.

If it comes back truncated, that is reported — the cap is declared by the step, and a
silently shortened excerpt would be worse than none.

## Gates

A step whose gate is `affirm` needs an authorisation you cannot produce yourself — see
the judgment rule on two turns. A gate of the form `preauth:<key>` may be satisfied by
configuration instead: set the key on the run, then record the decision as `preauth`.
Recording a preauth while its key is unset is refused; pre-authorisation is never
inferred.

## Variants

Some flows have more than one shape. It is pinned when the run opens and does not
change. Steps belonging to the other shape are not 'skippable' — they DO NOT EXIST, and
entering or skipping them is refused.

If a recorded value conflicts with the run's shape, the run was opened in the wrong
shape: close it and open a new one with the shape stated explicitly. Do NOT edit the
recorded value to match — that converts 'opened wrong' into 'the record says I did not'.

## Obligations

A hook whose condition matches raises an obligation. Closing the run is refused while
any remain undischarged. List them, do what the body says, then discharge each with
evidence of what you did. The body is in the store, so a truncated output cannot lose it.

## Guidance comes in tiers

`next` prints the directive unconditionally — a few lines, enough to act. It also prints
POINTERS to a longer guide and to named topics. Fetch those on demand.

## Optional steps

Some steps may legitimately never run. Record that decision rather than leaving them
open, or the run cannot be closed.

## Repeatable steps

Some steps may run more than once — a fix-and-recheck cycle. Some carry a budget; when
it is exhausted the engine records that fact rather than letting the loop continue
silently.

## Mutually exclusive steps

Some steps come in groups where exactly one member ever runs. Closing one satisfies the
group; its siblings are then not owed.

## Phase acceptance

A phase can carry a criterion of its own. Summarising a phase is refused when it is not
met. There is a read-only form of the same question — ask that first; it is faster than
attempting the summary and reading the refusal.

## Guards run outside your control

Certain tool calls are checked before they happen, and a missing authorisation stops
them with the BLOCKED code. That check is not something you invoke; it is wired into the
runtime hosting you.

## Judgment

These do not follow from the command surface. Each one is here because its absence
produced a specific failure.

### Saying a step is done is not what closes it

Record the evidence the step asks for, then close it. If the close is refused, the work is not finished — read what the refusal names and do that.

*Why:* The predicate is evaluated against the store, not against your account of it. This is the whole difference between a flow and a list of instructions.

### An affirmation takes two turns, never one

Put what needs deciding in front of the human and END your turn. Record the affirmation in the turn AFTER they answer.

*Why:* The engine counts whether a human spoke since the last one. Asking and answering inside a single turn is detected as forged and refused — and every refusal is kept.

### Read the answer, do not parse the prose

Pass --json on the commands you drive with and branch on the fields. The text beside it is for a person reading over your shoulder.

*Why:* A REFUSAL answers as data too — so the path that decides what you do next needs no parsing either. Wording is not a contract and changes without notice; the fields and the exit code are. Setup and the commands whose whole output is prose have no --json, and `--help` says which those are.

### Quote the human, do not summarise them

Put their own words in the evidence.

*Why:* A summary silently changes meaning: a conditional yes becomes an unconditional one, and the record then says something the human never said.

### Do not read all the guidance up front

The directive is enough to start. Fetch a guide or a topic only when you need it.

*Why:* A mature flow carries thousands of lines of guidance. Preloading it spends the context you need for the work, and the tiering exists precisely so you do not have to.

### A spec that blocks you is not a spec to edit

If a criterion cannot be met, say so. Never relax the criterion, and never rewrite a record so that a criterion passes.

*Why:* Both are the same move: turning 'the work is incomplete' into 'the record says it is complete'. The second is worse than the first, because it is invisible afterwards.

### Nothing forces you to open a run

When a task will change files or make an external effect, open a run FIRST.

*Why:* The runtime guard allows every action while no run is open — it runs before every tool call and must never brick a machine. The one exception is a scope someone has declared to REQUIRE a flow — in a record on the machine, or in a `.harness-required` file in the directory tree you are working in: there it refuses and names the run to open. Everywhere else skipping this is not blocked, and afterwards nothing distinguishes a flow that was followed from one that was never started.

## Never

- Force past owed work or undischarged obligations without asking the human first. Each
  force is recorded as a breach, and the two are separate authorisations — one does not
  cover the other.
- Edit the store directly. Every state change has a command; writing to it bypasses every
  check and leaves no trace that it happened.
- Reword an action to get past a BLOCKED result.

## Environment

| variable | effect |
|---|---|
| `HARNESS_ABILITIES_PATH` | where flows are searched for; os.pathsep-separated, REPLACES the default |
| `HARNESS_STATE_DIR` | where the store lives |
| `HARNESS_ACTOR` | who is driving — recorded for diagnosis, never used for isolation |

## Tools the runtime hook must cover

Derived from what the installed flows declare. A tool absent from the host's matcher
list is never checked, and that failure is silent — the declaration looks fine and the
hook is simply never asked.

```sh
CRAddComment
TaskeiCreateTask
TaskeiUpdateTask
shell
```

Not every guarded action is in that list. These are declared with no way for a
hook to recognise them in a tool call, so they are only ever checked when a caller
ASKS — `harness guard` — which means they depend on the driver choosing to ask:

```sh
delivery  close_task
delivery  commit
delivery  publish
```
